newsitem.title: UK: British utilities aim to offer value for money.
newsitem.headline: British utilities aim to offer value for money.

text.p: Britain's utility companies are aiming to win customers but at the same time boost company rewards with a variety of approaches, ahead of liberalisation of the country's gas and electricity markets in 1998, company executives said on Tuesday.
"We aim to add value in a way that means the customer gains and the company gains," Duncan Whyte, executive director of multi-utility at Scottish Power plc told a three-day utilities conference here.

He said Scottish Power, which owns regional electricity company (REC) Manweb and water firm Southern Water, had a strategy of diversifying into other utility businesses, expanding in those markets and taking opportunities in electricity internationally.

He said that "size and scale is important" for the company to maximise possibilities of offering efficiency savings, but added that "quality of service, quality of supply" were important factors as well as price.
Standards of service are the key factor for Centrica plc, according to Mike Alexander, managing director of Centrica's British Gas Trading (BGT).

"High standards of customer service will be the difference between winners and losers in the competitive market," he told the conference, which will hear from Clare Spottiswoode, head of the gas industry regulator Ofgas, on Wednesday.
"We won't be the cheapest gas supplier, but we will offer value for money," he added.

British Gas plc, now demerged into Centrica and BG plc, lost 85,000 customers during recent preliminary trials of a liberalised market in the south west of England, Brian Murphy, director of customer operations at BGT, told the conference.

Alexander said the aims for BGT to become a complete energy company included maximising customer loyalty, value for money, competitor differentiation and diversification from its core business, largely through alliances.

Eastern, the electricity business of the Energy Group plc, spun off from conglomerate Hanson earlier this year, sees its energy trading arm as the prime driver for profit growth, Jim Whelan, director of gas and energy management, said.

"The real synergies and the real possibilities for profit growth are in Super Trader," the arm of the company which manages risk and aims for arbitrage benefits of both producing and supplying electricity along with gas interests.

Whelan said he felt competition in Britain's generating market, where National Power plc and PowerGen plc were forced to sell capacity to the Hanson company by the government, had not gone far enough.
But he added that it could not be forced and with newer plants coming on stream should be "a fairly active generation market" by 2001 or 2002.

He said Eastern had no intention of moving into the water business as part of its multi-utility activities, adding that the company felt an integrated gas and electricity business "is the right format."

At Hyder plc, the Welsh electricity and water utility formed when Welsh Water took control of South Wales Electricity (Swalec) early in 1996, cost advantages which can deliver either lower prices or higher standards or both are "a decided advantage in a competitive market," John Roberts, chief executive of Swalec, said.
He said the key factors differentiating Hyder from its competitors were a strong management team, clear focus and shared customer base and support services between its utility arms.
"For a multi-utility to be a success, it must have many similarities and few differences," Roberts said.
